newsitem.title: CHINA: China to launch satellite on Long March 3B.
newsitem.headline: China to launch satellite on Long March 3B.

text.p: China plans to launch a satellite for the Philippines early next month in the first known use of its Long March 3B rocket since a disastrous explosion in February 1996.
The Mabuhay communications satellite would be launched between August 8 and 10, Chinese officials said on Monday.
"The coming launches will all basically use the 3B rocket because the thrust is greater," said Mao Di, chief engineer of the control centre for the Xichang satellite launch centre.
Mao was speaking to reporters who had been invited to view Xichang, the main commercial centre for satellite launches in China.
China plans four more commercial launches this year, making a total of six in 1997.
In February 1996 a Long March 3B rocket carrying a U.S.-built satellite for the Intelsat consortium blew up, killing at least six people.
China said an electrical problem linked to the direction-controlling inertial platform was to blame and had been corrected.
"I think the problem has been solved," Mao said. "The Long March 3B is reliable."
Chinese officials were reluctant to say categorically whether this would be the first use of the Long March 3B since the 1996 failure.
China launched a defence satellite this year and it was unknown which rocket was used.
The next launch after the Mabuhay satellite would be Apstar 2R for the Beijing-controlled Hong Kong firm APT Satellite Holdings Ltd. No exact date was given.
In January 1995 a Long March 2E rocket carrying the original Apstar 2 satellite blew up shortly after lift-off.
China has been under fire for fatalities in the past launches. Successful launches would go a long way to restoring confidence in its commercial space programme.
"I think it's okay," said another official at the launch site, referring to the 3B rocket.
"The structure is pretty good," he said.
"If we have any safety problem we can blow the rocket up," said Mao. "We have a vehicle destruction system. By this we can avoid the launch vehicle endangering life or property."
Industry sources have said the Apstar launch could be in September.
Officials declined to discuss insurance rates for the launch, although Mao did say insurance premiums were going up for all commercial launches because costs were rising.
